intro: Mahler’s Ninth grows from a broken rhythm and a two-note sigh into an immense first movement. Bruno Walter conducts the Vienna Philharmonic in 1938, in the hall where he gave its première in 1912.

sections.mNote: Cellos, horn and harp precede the second violins’ D-major tune

sections.label: B · The music turns minor
sections.mNote: A darker, impassioned passage, soon over

cues.title: A rhythm finding its feet
cues.text: Cellos begin a halting rhythm, pp, and a horn completes it, stopped and then marked offen (Echo). The harp answers at f with firmer steps, a double bass holds a harmonic, and the violas begin to rock. Mahler starts with separate voices, each leaving room for the next.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, Universal Edition first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 1: Andante comodo; cellos pp, horns p with gest. and offen (Echo), harp f, double bass Flag. pp, violas pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song in short phrases
cues.text: At rehearsal 1 the second violins begin a melody in short segments separated by rests, full of small falling sighs. Divided violas rock beneath it in sextuplets, and cellos and basses pluck the steps.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 1–2: rehearsal 1, second violins with the melody, divided violas in sextuplets, cellos and basses pizzicato. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the exposition commences with a lyrical violin melody made up of short segments separated by rests, with descending sigh figures: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Walter returns to the Musikverein
cues.text: Vienna, 16 January 1938. Bruno Walter stands before the orchestra that gave the Ninth its première under him in June 1912, in this same Musikverein hall. Mahler never heard the symphony; he died a year before that first performance.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, pp. 1–2, on the première, recording and shared venue. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: D major turns minor
cues.text: After only a few minutes the music moves into the minor for a darker, impassioned passage. It proves short-lived: a quasi-fanfare in the trumpets brings back the opening material in heightened form.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: after only a few minutes the music moves into the minor mode for a darker, impassioned passage, which proves short-lived, and a quasi-fanfare in the trumpets marks a heightened return of the opening material: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/ . Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 5: one-flat signature, trumpets f cresc. before a Rit.

cues.title: A falling second, and Les Adieux
cues.text: Every movement of the Ninth is built on a falling second, from the third to the second step of the scale. Those are the first two notes of Beethoven’s Das Lebewohl Sonata, Op. 81a. In 1875 Mahler’s father let his fifteen-year-old son study in Vienna after the boy had played that sonata.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile of the original draft of the first three movements describes the motto, the link to Beethoven’s Op. 81a and Mahler’s father’s decision of 1875: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Mahler-Symphony-No.-9-Original-draft-of-1st-3-Movements.-Facsimile-of-Composers-Manuscript-D-major-for-orchestra/P0005537

cues.title: A chord that settles nothing
cues.text: The exposition ends on a great chord from the whole orchestra, and then everything dies away over a timpani roll that falls from ff to pp. No goal has been reached.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 16: sustained chord in the winds and brass, timpani roll ff dim. to pp, then Tempo I subito (aber nicht schleppend). Basinger: brass fanfares drive the section to its climax, at which point the exposition comes to its close: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horns remember
cues.text: Tempo I subito (aber nicht schleppend) — back to the first tempo, but without dragging. Horns and trombones, muted, bring back motives from the opening bars over a timpani roll, pp, and the lyrical tune appears only in fragments.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 16: Tempo I subito (aber nicht schleppend), horns, trombones mit Dämpfer, bass tuba, timpani roll pp. Basinger: timpani rolls and low brass, playing motives from the opening moments, indicate the start of the development, alternating with fragments of the lyrical melody amid stopped horns, muted trombones and the tam-tam: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two machines beside the timpani
cues.text: Producer Fred Gaisberg sits near the timpani, facing Walter. Two machines take turns cutting the performance into wax: one records while the other is reloaded. Beside the engineer, a musician follows the full score, keeping the joins clear of the music’s path.
cues.evidence: Gaisberg’s account of the 1938 session, quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 2. It describes his seat, the alternating wax-disc machines and the musician following the score.

cues.title: A waltz for lost youth
cues.text: The violins bring in a gentle tune that quotes Johann Strauss’s waltz Freuet euch des Lebens, written in 1870 for the opening ball of the Musikverein’s new golden hall, in the building of the Conservatory where Mahler studied. It returns twice more.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile (Reinhold Kubik, May 2009, drawing on Stephen Hefling) names the three quotations of the Strauss waltz (bars 148ff., 267–271 and 436ff.), the waltz’s history and the Conservatory in the same building: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Symphony-No.-9-Draft-Score-of-the-First-Three-Movements/P0005537
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trumpets stand fast
cues.text: Muted trumpets quietly play triplet figures. The orchestra swells: timpani rolls, violin trills, horns marked gestopft climbing to fff, until at Mit Wut the full orchestra erupts.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 22–23: trumpets mit Dämpfer in triplets p, timpani roll, trills in the second violins, molto cresc., horns gest. fff; p. 23 Mit Wut. Allegro risoluto. Basinger: the tune soars until fanfares signal significant contrast; the full orchestra then presents the main theme mit Wut: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Mit Wut”
cues.text: At rehearsal 9 Mahler writes Mit Wut, with rage, and Allegro risoluto, but not too fast. The horns are marked immer gestopft, always stopped; they snarl beside open trumpets while the strings fight in dissonant counterpoint.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition first-edition score, printed p. 23, rehearsal 9: Mit Wut. Allegro risoluto (Nicht zu schnell), horns immer gestopft: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP353450-PMLP48640-Mahler_Symphony_9_.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cry, then a collapse
cues.text: A cymbal stroke, swells in the harps and a sweeping horn line carry the music to a brilliant, dissonant peak. At rehearsal 11 the key signature changes to E♭ major, and rapid chromatic runs plunge through violas, cellos and basses as the orchestra collapses.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 28–29: Becken ff, harp runs, rehearsal 11 with a change of key signature, rapid descending figures in violas, cellos and basses, ff dim. Basinger: swells in the harp, a sudden switch to the major mode and a sweeping horn line lead to a brilliant, if dissonant, peak; an immediate collapse follows: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings in the shadows
cues.text: Mahler writes Schattenhaft — shadowy. Horns sigh above muted trombones while the violas, cellos and basses rock in whispered sextuplets. Then Allmählich an Ton gewinnend — gradually gaining in tone — and the lyrical tune begins to come back in D major.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 35: Schattenhaft, horns offen and immer Sord. in the trombones, ppp strings in sextuplets, two sharps, Allmählich an Ton gewinnend. Basinger: a schattenhaft indication appears as the horns continue their sighs above muted trombones, and the lyrical melody then rises again: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “O days of youth!”
cues.text: Over the Strauss waltz in the draft Mahler writes, in the score itself: “O Jugendzeit! Entschwundene! O Liebe! Verwehte!” — oh, days of youth, vanished; oh, love, scattered on the wind.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile: at the most prominent citation of the Strauss waltz (bars 267–271) Mahler wrote these words into the score: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Mahler-Symphony-No.-9-Original-draft-of-1st-3-Movements.-Facsimile-of-Composers-Manuscript-D-major-for-orchestra/P0005537

cues.title: A presentiment of death
cues.text: Alban Berg writes to his wife that this whole movement is “a presentiment of death”. It “appears again and again”, he says, and “all that is earthly and dreamy culminates in it”.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile (Reinhold Kubik, May 2009) quotes Berg’s letter to his wife, written in 1923 or later: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Symphony-No.-9-Draft-Score-of-the-First-Three-Movements/P0005537

cues.title: A dissonance mit höchster Gewalt
cues.text: Trombones and tuba, bells raised, hammer a dissonance marked fff (mit höchster Gewalt) — with the greatest force — with the timpani, while woodwinds and strings tumble downward in rapid figures. The score says Stringendo just before it.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 45: Stringendo; trombones and bass tuba fff (mit höchster Gewalt), Schalltr. auf., timpani ff, rapid descending figures in woodwinds and strings. Basinger: woodwinds and strings descend over a strident dissonance in timpani and low brass, mit höchster Gewalt: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Like a funeral procession
cues.text: The blow leads into a march marked Wie ein schwerer Kondukt, like a heavy funeral procession, over a timpani ostinato. Three deep bells join the timpani.
cues.evidence: Score, movement I, pp. 47–48 (IMSLP #353450): Wie ein schwerer Kondukt over timpani, and a staff for 3 tiefe Glocken on p. 48: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP353450-PMLP48640-Mahler_Symphony_9_.pdf . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the development proceeds “wie ein schwerer Kondukt”, trumpet fanfares sound and bells ring: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whose heartbeat?
cues.text: Leonard Bernstein heard Mahler’s irregular heartbeat in the opening rhythm. The rhythm keeps returning in the score; at the movement’s crisis, trombones and tuba hammer it out mit höchster Gewalt, with the greatest force.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement reports Bernstein’s suggestion that the opening motif depicts Mahler’s irregular heartbeat: https://www.mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-1-andante-comodo/ . The rhythm’s return in the trombones and tuba, marked Mit höchster Gewalt, is in the score of the movement.

cues.title: Birdcalls
cues.text: Plötzlich bedeutend langsamer (Lento) und leise, Misterioso: the music drops to a hush. Piccolo, flute, oboes and a solo violin weave delicate lines that commentators hear as birdcalls.
cues.evidence: Score, movement I, p. 54 (IMSLP #353450), two pages before the coda’s Schon ganz langsam on p. 56: Plötzlich bedeutend langsamer (Lento) und leise, Misterioso, with small flute, flute, oboes, English horn, clarinet, horns, solo violin and viola: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP353450-PMLP48640-Mahler_Symphony_9_.pdf . The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes the passage as birdcall polyphony: https://www.mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-1-andante-comodo/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A horn opens the coda
cues.text: Schon ganz langsam — already very slow. A horn, marked molto espr. and sehr weich hervortretend — very softly to the fore — sings in D major; harp arpeggios rise beneath held wind chords and the strings fade to a few notes.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 56: Schon ganz langsam, two sharps, first horn molto espr. p (sehr weich hervortretend), trombones pp, harp arpeggios, sparse strings. Basinger: all elements of the exposition recur, varied, before the movement fades out in a coda: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A solo violin at the end
cues.text: The closing melody passes to a solo violin, marked schmeichelnd — coaxing — and later dolciss. The harp climbs; horns and woodwinds answer softly. At the last bar, Zögernd, the strings pluck harmonics on the G string, pp, under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 58: Wieder a tempo (aber viel langsamer als zu Anfang), solo violin schmeichelnd, espr., Zögernd, dolciss.; harp ascending; last bar pizzicato Flag. auf der G-Saite pp with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The music turns minor
transitions.from: A · A broken rhythm becomes a song
transitions.how: After only a few minutes the D-major song gives way to the minor for a darker, impassioned passage. It proves short-lived: a quasi-fanfare in the trumpets brings back the opening material in heightened form.
transitions.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the music moves into the minor mode for a darker, impassioned passage; a quasi-fanfare in the trumpets marks a heightened return of the opening material: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

transitions.title: A timpani roll fades
transitions.to: Dev · Horns and timpani recall the opening
transitions.how: The exposition ends on a great chord. A timpani roll survives it and fades from ff to pp. At Tempo I subito horns and muted trombones bring back motives from the opening bars.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 16. Basinger: timpani rolls and low brass, playing motives from the opening, mark the start of the development.

transitions.title: Trumpets set the orchestra swelling
transitions.from: Dev · Horns and timpani recall the opening
transitions.to: Dev · Muted trumpets, then Mit Wut
transitions.how: Muted trumpets play quiet triplets, and the orchestra swells with timpani rolls, trills and stopped horns rising to fff. At Mit Wut. Allegro risoluto, with horns immer gestopft, the full orchestra presents the main theme.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 22–23. Basinger: the full orchestra presents the main theme mit Wut, fortissimo, with stopped and muted brass.

transitions.title: Schattenhaft
transitions.from: Dev · Muted trumpets, then Mit Wut
transitions.how: A fermata, and then Schattenhaft: horns sigh above muted trombones while the low strings rock in whispered sextuplets. Allmählich an Ton gewinnend, the D-major tune begins to return.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 35. Basinger: a schattenhaft indication appears as the horns continue their sighs above muted trombones.

transitions.title: A dissonance in trombones and tuba
transitions.to: Link · A dissonance in low brass
transitions.how: At Stringendo the orchestra presses forward, and woodwinds and strings tumble downward. Trombones and tuba strike a dissonance marked fff (mit höchster Gewalt) with the timpani.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 45. Basinger: woodwinds and strings descend over a strident dissonance played by timpani and low brass, mit höchster Gewalt.

transitions.title: The opening comes back
transitions.from: Link · A dissonance in low brass
transitions.how: The development goes on wie ein schwerer Kondukt, with muted trumpets and bells. Then, at Wie von Anfang, the opening returns: harp, plucked low strings and timpani under horns and woodwinds, marked espress.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 47–49: Wie ein schwerer Kondukt, tiefe Glocken, Wie von Anfang with harp, pizzicato basses and horns. Basinger: trumpet fanfares sound and bells ring, the horn sighs persist, and the lyrical melody returns.

transitions.title: The coda begins
transitions.to: Coda · Horn, harp and solo violin
transitions.how: At Schon ganz langsam a horn sings molto espr., harp arpeggios rise beneath held wind chords, and the strings thin out to a few notes.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 56.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement I, printed pp. 1–58: cello, horn and harp opening; second-violin first theme; low-brass climax; horn, harp and solo violin in the coda.

timeline.note: Cellos begin the hesitant rhythm and the fourth horn completes it.
Harp notes and horn calls sound above the violas’ rocking thirds.
Second violins grow their melody from a falling second above divided strings.
First violins push upwards with the sharper D-minor theme.
Horns and timpani recover the opening rhythms among low winds and strings.
Trombones and tuba enlarge the opening rhythm above the rushing strings.
A long horn phrase unfolds over held winds, harp arpeggios and rocking cellos.
Flute and solo violin carry exposed lines between quiet wind and harp replies.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
